# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may freeze out entirely. On a tidally locked exoplanet, the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night—may host the only temperate conditions.

However, tidal locking doesn't necessarily doom a planet to climatic extremes. If a planet retains a substantial atmosphere, winds redistribute heat from dayside to nightside. Climate models of worlds like those orbiting red dwarfs suggest that ocean planets with thick atmospheres could maintain surprisingly temperate conditions across much of their surface.
